title: SDG 4 Through Relational Pedagogy: Latino Students’ Experiences of Belonging, Mentorship, and Inclusion
abstract: This article reinterprets findings from a previously completed qualitative bounded case study of seven Dominican, Puerto Rican, and Mexican college students from the Bronx through the framework of Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4). No new empirical data were collected for the present article. The original study examined how participants experienced meaningful teacher–student relationships across their educational journeys. Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) serves as the principal interpretive framework, while familioso, used here as an emerging culturally grounded relational lens informed by familismo, helps illuminate family-like qualities of trust, belonging, mentorship, advocacy, mutual responsibility, and sustained support within educational relationships. The original study identified six themes concerning mentorship and identity development, relational learning communities, negotiated authority and authenticity, family-like relational structures, family cultural values, and cultural identity. Reinterpreted through SDG 4, these findings suggest that educational quality is experienced not only through structural conditions and academic opportunities but also throu

title: Navigating Disruption: A Transformative Learning Theory Examination of Faculty Perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Academic Practices
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have rapidly entered higher education, challenging longstanding norms around authorship, assessment, and disciplinary expertise. While early GenAI scholarship has largely emphasized student outcomes, adoption trends, and academic integrity, comparatively little empirical work has examined how faculty and staff make sense of this disruption over time. Guided by Transformative Learning Theory (TLT) as an interpretive lens for faculty discourse, this qualitative study examines how educators interpret GenAI as a “disorienting dilemma” and how patterns in faculty discourse differ across two cross-sectional cohorts during the first year of widespread adoption. We analyzed open-ended survey responses to the question, “How do you think AI tools like ChatGPT will impact the future of your discipline?” collected at a large U.S. R1 Hispanic-serving public research university. Two cohorts were examined: an early-adoption dataset gathered in 2023 (n = 104) and a follow-up dataset collected in 2024 (n = 313). Using Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis procedures, we identified persistent themes and qualitative differences

title: From Teacher Education to Middle Leadership: Developing Equity-Oriented Leadership in Primary Science Education
abstract: Equitable science education in primary schools depends on whether all pupils can participate meaningfully in the distinctive practices of science, including inquiry, practical investigation, observation, evidence-based discussion, fieldwork, and the use of specialist resources. Yet access to these experiences can be uneven, as primary teachers vary in confidence, subject knowledge, resources, and preparation for organising science-rich learning. While research has examined primary teachers’ preparedness to teach science, less attention has been given to how primary science middle leaders develop the capacity to support equitable science teaching and learning across their schools. This study explores how primary science middle leaders understand and enact equity-oriented leadership in relation to science curriculum, pedagogy, resources, assessment, and pupil participation. Using semi-structured interviews with fifteen primary science subject leaders working in English primary schools, data were analysed thematically to identify factors shaping science-specific leadership capacity. Findings show that leaders foster equitable primary science by supporting inquiry and practical work, p

title: Does Shared Reading Promote Cognitive Development? A Literature Review
abstract: Shared reading is recognized as an educational method that promotes language development and emergent literacy during early childhood. However, growing evidence suggests that it influences additional developmental domains. This review examined empirical and theoretical literature with the aim of uncovering the potential of shared reading as an inclusive pedagogical approach for supporting children’s cognitive development by integrating findings on adult mediation, dialogic interaction, repeated reading, mental state discourse, instructional adaptations, and shared reading across diverse learner populations. The reviewed literature indicates that the effectiveness of shared reading depends primarily on the quality of the adult–child interaction. Adult mediation, instructional scaffolding, collaborative dialogue, and active child participation were found to be key instruments for supporting learning across home, preschool, and inclusive educational settings. Studies involving children with developmental disabilities, autism spectrum disorder, deafness, and deafblindness indicate that adapted shared reading promotes participation and advances language, communication, and broader devel

title: Conceptualizing School Leaders as Organizers of Systems and Resources
abstract: This study examined distributed leadership at a school that underwent transformation over a ten-year period beginning in 2014. Building on theory, we focused on capacity building as a key construct in distributed leadership, connecting it to the vision for school transformation and to the distribution of responsibilities outside central administration. We explored how this vision was enacted within the mathematics department, aiming to understand how educators translate theoretical notions of distributed leadership into a site-specific vision at the department level. We developed a leadership model with three interlocking components: visioning and revisioning, building capacity, and exercising autonomy with accountability. Using four protocols, we conducted 27 interviews with 19 participants, analyzing to generate themes. Initial visioning encountered implementation tensions, prompting revisioning around four tenets. The vision of a less hierarchical decision-making process entailed creating a teacher leader position, whose responsibilities included leading curriculum development and instructional reform. title: Higher Education Institution Choice: A Systematic Review of Contemporary Trends and Decision Factors
abstract: Higher education institution (HEI) choice is increasingly influenced by digitalisation, internationalisation, intensified institutional competition, widening participation, and financial uncertainty. This study systematically reviews how institution choice has been conceptualised and examined across domestic and international contexts. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 56 English-language, open-access studies indexed in Scopus were analysed through descriptive mapping and thematic synthesis, with the literature search last updated on 17 September 2026. The review examined publication and methodological patterns, geographical contexts, student populations, research directions, theoretical foundations and reported choice factors. The methodological profile comprised 23 qualitative, 22 quantitative, and eight mixed-methods studies among the 53 empirical publications. Within the selected corpus of 56 studies, the literature is geographically concentrated, while comparative studies are limited. title: Curriculum-Aligned AR for Secondary Physics: Learning and Engagement in Circular Motion and Magnetic Force
abstract: Static diagrams inherently flatten the dynamic, three-dimensional interplay of forces and motion, leaving secondary students reliant on imagination to grasp invisible vectors—a challenge consistently documented in high-stakes physics examinations. While augmented reality (AR) offers a promising medium to externalise these abstractions, rigorous classroom evidence comparing theory-driven, curriculum-aligned AR with standard instructional materials remains scarce. Grounded in Variation Theory, Cognitive Load Theory, and Constructivism, this study evaluated a smartphone-based AR application featuring seven 3-D models tightly mapped to the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) physics syllabus. Evaluating N = 171 Form 4 students (Grade 10 equivalent, aged 15–16) across nine classes in seven secondary schools, we employed a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test crossover design comparing AR against equivalent textbook images. title: Digital Skill Alignment over Time: The Dynamic Digital Skill Realisation Framework for Graduate Employability
abstract: Higher education is expected to develop digital capabilities that support graduate employability, but the labour-market relevance of those capabilities can change between acquisition and employment entry. This conceptual article develops the Dynamic Digital Skill Realisation Framework (DDSRF) to explain that transition as a time-sensitive process rather than a fixed skills match. A theory-building synthesis was constructed through targeted purposive searches spanning higher education, digital skills, graduate employability, labour-market alignment, skill decay and obsolescence, signalling, employer judgement, and unequal employment outcomes. The contribution lies not in introducing new individual constructs, but in integrating them into a temporally explicit process. The framework distinguishes capability formation from initial alignment, capability-side skill decay from demand-side obsolescence, and skill signalling from employer recognition and valuation. It further specifies how contextual conditions shape the conversion of recognised skill value into realised employability outcomes and how graduate outcomes can inform institutional renewal. title: Social–Emotional Competence Across Arab Educational Subsystems in Israel: A Comparative Analysis of Sector, Gender and SES
abstract: Social–emotional competence (SEC) is an important factor contributing to students’ academic success and psychological well-being. While research on SEC is widespread, studies within the unique demographic and ethnic context of the Arab minority in Israel remain scarce. This study examined SEC levels across three distinct educational subsystems (General Arab, Druze, and Bedouin), alongside gender and socioeconomic status (SES). A sample of 852 fifth- and sixth-grade students was recruited from 15 elementary schools in northern Israel. SEC was evaluated using an adapted 40-item self-report online questionnaire split into emotional and social subscales. A 3 × 2 factorial ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of the educational subsystem, with post hoc pairwise comparisons showing that Druze students scored significantly higher than both General Arab and Bedouin students. Intriguingly, independent t-tests revealed no significant differences in SEC based on gender, grade level or SES. These results suggest that cultural–ethnic background and distinct institutional contexts serve as the primary sources of variance in SEC in this cohort. title: Perceived Institutional Digital Education Conditions and Self-Reported Pedagogical Innovation at a Peruvian University
abstract: Digital education is now a core institutional condition of higher education, but technology access alone does not describe pedagogical practice. This study examines the association between perceived institutional digital education conditions and self-reported pedagogical innovation-related practice among 65 Business Administration faculty members at one private university in Huancayo, Peru. A quantitative cross-sectional survey used two study-specific 35-item Likert-type instruments. title: Teacher Wastage in Pakistan: How Education Systems Employ Teachers but Lose Instructional Capacity
abstract: Pakistan has expanded teacher recruitment across its public education system over the past decade, yet policy and monitoring reports continue to document substantial rural, school-level, and subject-specific teacher shortages. In this article, I extend the concept of educational wastage to teachers, shifting attention from the loss of teachers to the loss or underuse of instructional capacity among formally employed teachers. I identify three forms of teacher wastage. Pre-deployment wastage occurs when appointment does not result in classroom instruction because teachers cannot take up or sustain placements, political influence directs placements away from school staffing needs, or teachers recorded as employed do not teach. Structural wastage occurs when teachers in schools are diverted from or misaligned with instruction through transfer instability, non-academic duties, or subject or grade-level misassignment. Erosive wastage occurs when teachers remain employed but lack adequate pedagogical preparation, induction, mentoring, or continuing professional support. title: Discursive Legitimation and Operational Threshold of Gender in Initial Teacher Education in Chilean Physical Education
abstract: Gender perspective (GP) has gained increasing legitimacy in initial teacher education, although challenges remain regarding its translation into conceptually grounded practices. In Physical Education (PE), the issue is particularly relevant due to the persistence of a masculinized disciplinary tradition and the centrality of the body. This study analyses how, in the discourse of teacher educators from two Chilean PE programs, the importance attributed to GP and the declared actions to implement it are distributed. A descriptive qualitative study was conducted using quantitative-oriented content analysis of 40 semi-structured interviews, corresponding to the entire eligible teaching staff. A total of 184 statements were analysed with a deductive category system. Of these, 63.1% referred to the importance attributed to GP and 36.9% to declared actions. Within the latter, 47.1% corresponded to inclusive language, 39.7% to practical strategies, and only 13.2% to theoretical-problematizing strategies, declared by seven of the 40 participants (17.5%). title: Effects of Predictive Reading Strategies on Reading Speed and Comprehension: Evidence from Non-English Major EFL Learners
abstract: The skill of reading effectively can be viewed as an important academic requirement. The investigation aims to explore the impact of predictive reading strategy instruction on the reading speed and reading comprehension of Computer Engineering students learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL).This study employed a quasi-experimental research method to conduct the investigation among 120 undergraduate EFL students in Shandong Province, China. The participants were divided into two groups, including an experimental group that received predictive reading strategy instruction and a control group that received conventional reading instruction for eight weeks. This study gathered data using three assessment tools, including a reading speed test, a reading comprehension test, and a Predictive Strategy Use Questionnaire. The researchers used descriptive statistics and Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) as the main statistical methods for the analysis. The results showed that predictive reading strategy instruction led to significant improvements in reading speed, reading comprehension, and predictive strategy use. title: Scenario-Based Learning for Teachers: A Multimethod Usability Study
abstract: Background: Teaching is a complex occupation that requires rapid decision-making across a variety of situations. Online, scenario-based professional development platforms can reach diverse users without facilitator support, making strong usability especially critical. However, formative evaluations of their usability and fit with teachers’ learning needs are rare. This study examines the usability of PRF4TeachersTM, an online scenario-based professional learning platform designed to support K-8 teachers to develop their instructional skills. Methods: Using a multimethod design, quantitative and qualitative data were collected in parallel and analyzed separately without integration. Participants were 18 female teachers (M = 8.24 yrs of experience, SD = 8.71), predominantly European American (61.1%) and teaching K-5th (66.7%) or 6–8th grade (33.3%). The System Usability Scale provided an overall index of teachers’ experience with the platform, while think-aloud and semi-structured interviews yielded component-specific feedback. title: Exploring University Students’ Experiences of Using Conversational Artificial Intelligence for Emotional and Relational Support in Experiences of Loneliness
abstract: University students’ loneliness has remained a persistent concern in the years following the COVID-19 pandemic and correlates with multiple mental health issues, yet little is known about how university students experiencing loneliness use conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) for emotional and relational support. This exploratory qualitative study addressed that gap by exploring how students in a UK university experiencing loneliness perceived their use of CAI for emotional and relational support, and how they positioned CAI alongside other coping strategies. Sixteen students scoring 3 or above on the De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. title: Teacher Mental Health and Well-Being from the Pandemic to the Post-Pandemic Era: A Systematic Review of Interventions, Policies, and Persistent Gaps
abstract: Teachers’ mental health problems have remained persistently elevated since the pandemic, yet system-level responses remain structurally inadequate. This systematic review synthesizes 66 peer-reviewed studies and policy reports (2020–2026). Meta-analyses of 54 studies (256,896 teachers, 22 countries) found stress prevalence at 62.6%, anxiety at 36.3%, and depression at 59.9%. Longitudinal evidence shows no recovery across 2021–2026; teachers fare worse than comparable professionals on all well-being indicators. Interventions show moderate effects (g = 0.42; trim-and-fill-adjusted g = 0.34), but the latter is an exploratory sensitivity analysis suggesting small-study effects, not a precise publication-bias estimate. Out of 24 intervention studies, 91.7% target individual-level coping; no peer-reviewed quantitative study evaluates macro-structural reforms. We propose the Evidence Hierarchy Mismatch Theory (EHMT) as one plausible explanation, alongside competing explanations. We introduce a three-tier framework (macro–meso–micro) extending the job demands–resources model with structural–social justice considerations. title: When Nature-Based Activities Become Participatory: Pedagogical Mediation of Young Children’s Participation
abstract: Child participation is central to rights-based early childhood education, yet it is often interpreted as verbal expression, choice-making or general engagement. Nature-based activities may broaden young children’s participation because they offer sensory, material and spatial forms of expression. Their participatory quality, however, depends on pedagogical mediation. This qualitative study analysed 24 interviews with preschool teachers in Latvia to examine how nature-based activities were described as becoming participatory in early childhood education. Deductive–inductive codebook thematic analysis was guided by six participation dimensions: access to information, being listened to, expressing views, discussing relevant matters, influence on decisions and independent decision-making. Findings identified four linked pedagogical processes: making participation possible through sensory and material access to information; recognising participation in children’s non-verbal and multimodal expressions; making participation consequential by allowing children’s ideas to affect materials, time and activity direction; and supporting agency through scaffolded decision-making and manageable co

title: Game Development-Based Learning for Early Programming Education Using Scratch and the [ai] Explore! Game
abstract: This study examines programming achievement among Grade 4 students participating in a structured Game Development-Based Learning (GDBL) approach compared with students receiving traditional programming instruction. The intervention used a single coherent problem context derived from the [ai] explore! game to support the progressive introduction of programming concepts in Scratch. A total of 104 students aged 9–10 from five classes in a Croatian elementary school participated. Two classes were assigned to the experimental condition and three to the control condition. Students in the experimental group progressively developed a playable game over seven weeks, while the control group followed traditional programming instruction. An initial knowledge test was used to assess baseline programming knowledge, and a post-intervention assessment served as the primary outcome measure. Because the instructional condition was assigned at the class level, the primary analysis used an exact class-level randomization test.
